title: Permanent Grab Bars for the Shower, Tub and Toilet: Why Screw-In Beats Suction
subtitle: A grab bar is one of the simplest bathroom safety upgrades, but only if it is anchored into the wall the right way.
excerpt: Suction-cup bars look like safety gear, but an installers' group says they are not a substitute for an anchored bar. Here is how permanent grab bars work, what to look for, and two Delta options, with prices to confirm at Home Depot.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: The bathroom asks a lot of our balance. We step over a tub edge onto a wet floor, turn around in a narrow shower, and lower ourselves onto a toilet seat and push back up again. It is easy to end up reaching for whatever is nearby, like a towel bar, a soap dish or the edge of the sink. Those fixtures are not meant to be leaned on, and a towel bar is not a substitute for a grab bar.

A grab bar is a sturdy handle fixed to the wall, made for exactly that job. It is not fancy and it does not need batteries or an app. But it only works if it is put up properly, and that is where mistakes are easy to make.
How a grab bar actually holds you

A grab bar is only as strong as what it is attached to. Tile, cement board and ordinary drywall cannot handle the sideways pull of someone putting their full weight on a bar. The screws need to go into a wall stud (the wooden or metal posts inside the wall), into solid wood blocking added behind the wall, or into special anchors rated for grab bars.

That is why suction-cup bars are a different thing altogether. Some sources say they can come loose under load. The Grab Bar Installers Association of America, a national group that certifies installers, said in a 2026 report that suction-cup bars sold in safety aisles carry packaging that disclaims the weight-bearing use their shape suggests. The group calls for a properly anchored bar in every shower and says suction bars are not a substitute for one. We have relied on summaries of that report, not the full text, so check the group's own guide if you want the details.

You may also see bars labeled "ADA compliant." That refers to the Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility standards. One general reference, citing the 2010 ADA Standards, says such bars and their mounts should withstand more than 250 pounds of force. Check the official standard if you need the exact requirement. Bars in a private home do not have to be ADA compliant, but the guidelines are worth considering. A weight rating is a strength test of the bar and its mounting, not a promise about any particular person's weight.

items: Screw-mounted, not suction. Look for a bar that fastens into studs, blocking or rated anchors.

A clear strength rating. Delta lists its bars below as supporting up to 450 pounds, and one caregiver guide suggests a rating of at least 250 pounds. Treat any rating as a structural figure, not a guarantee for a user's weight.
Where the screws will land. Home Depot says studs are typically 16 or 24 inches apart, so check where studs sit before choosing a length.
Rust resistance. Stainless steel with a protective finish is a sensible choice for a wet shower.
Installation cost. The bar's price is only part of the bill. Ask for an installation quote before you buy if you are not doing it yourself.
Returns and permission. Check the store's return policy, and if you rent, get your landlord's approval before drilling.

sections.content: Putting it up and using it well

If you are comfortable with tools, the job calls for a stud finder, a drill with a tile bit if you are going through tile, and stainless screws. If there is no stud where you need the bar, you will need blocking or grab-bar anchors, and that can mean opening the wall. Home Depot links to installation services from its product pages, though a price is not listed there, so ask for a quote. A handyman or contractor who has installed grab bars before is often worth the money.

Think about where your hands naturally go. Common spots are beside the tub or shower entrance, on the long wall inside the shower, and next to the toilet. Home Depot's installation guide suggests horizontal bars near toilets go 33 to 36 inches from the floor, but check the right height for your bathroom with an installer. Look over the bar every so often for wobble. If it moves, stop using it and have it checked. Please do not test it with your full body weight.

A grab bar helps with balance, but a bar alone may not be enough for anyone who needs full-body support. If getting up from the toilet takes real effort, a raised seat with arms or a toilet frame may be needed as well, and a tub bench can help with getting in and out of the bath. A doctor, physical therapist or occupational therapist can suggest what fits your needs. In an emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A well-anchored grab bar is a modest purchase that can do its job for years. Take the time to mount it into something solid, put it where your hands already reach, and you will have a steady hand in the bathroom whenever you need one.
